## [Part 3: Large Language Models - Internal Workings]{style="color:#154360;"}
### [From architecture to domain adaptation]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
- 🏗️ **Stacked Transformer blocks**: multi-head attention + feed-forward  
- ⚙️ **Feed-Forward Layers**: non-linear transformations per position  
- 🧠 **Multi-Head Attention**: learn multiple context types simultaneously  
:::

::: notes
Part 3 begins by opening the “black box” of an LLM to see how a single Transformer block processes information. Multi-head attention allows the model to focus on several context aspects in parallel—capturing syntax here, semantics there, and domain cues elsewhere. Feed-forward layers then apply non-linear transformations to each token embedding, enriching its representation. Residual connections and layer normalization ensure stable gradients and faster convergence, allowing us to stack many such blocks to build deep, powerful models.
:::

---

## [General vs Medical-Specific Models]{style="color:#1A5276;"}
### [Adaptation for clinical knowledge]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
- 🤖 **General LLMs**: ChatGPT, Claude, Llama — broad web training  
- 🏥 **Medical LLMs**: LiVersa, PathChat, BrainGPT — fine-tuned on clinical corpora  
- 🔍 **Challenges**: domain-specific terminology, ontology integration, privacy  
:::

::: notes
General-purpose LLMs like ChatGPT and Llama are trained on broad web corpora, giving them impressive general language understanding but limited depth in niche domains. In contrast, medical-specific models such as LiVersa, PathChat, or BrainGPT incorporate clinical notes, peer-reviewed research, and standardized ontologies to master terminology, clinical reasoning, and privacy constraints. This fine-tuning process boosts accuracy, reduces domain-specific hallucinations, and imbues the model with specialized knowledge required for healthcare applications.
:::

## [Interpretability & Limitations]{style="color:#884EA0;"}
### [Hallucinations, Bias, and Safety]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="columns"}
:::: {.column width="60%" style="font-size:0.85em;"}
- 🌈 **Hallucinations**: confident but incorrect outputs  
- ⚖️ **Bias**: learned from skewed training data (e.g., demographic bias)  
- 🔒 **Privacy & Compliance**: sensitive patient data concerns  
:::
:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: comments
Suggest an image showing hallucination phenomenon: e.g., a model confidently answering a question incorrectly.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
It’s crucial to recognize that LLMs, despite their power, are not perfect. Hallucinations occur when models confidently generate incorrect or fabricated details—imagine a model inventing drug doses that don’t exist. Bias may emerge from skewed training data, potentially leading to unequal performance across patient groups. Moreover, any use of patient data demands strict compliance with privacy regulations like GDPR or HIPAA; models and infrastructure should anonymize sensitive fields and safeguard data at rest and in transit.
:::

## [Part 4: LLM in Chat vs API]{style="color:#C0392B;"}
### [Choosing your interface]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
- 💬 **Chat Interface**: interactive, context maintained, user-friendly  
- 🔗 **API Access**: programmable, batch processing, integration in pipelines  
- ⚖️ **Trade-offs**: latency, cost per call, data residency, customization  
:::

::: notes
Chat-based interfaces excel at interactive exploration, letting clinicians iterate prompts, clarify context, and obtain immediate narrative responses without writing code. APIs, on the other hand, are designed for automation, batch processing, and seamless embedding into electronic health record systems or lab pipelines. When choosing between them, weigh factors such as response latency, volume-based cost, data residency requirements, and the level of customization or logging needed for auditing clinical decisions.

## [Key Takeaways: Part 3]{style="color:#154360;"}
### [Summary of LLM Internals and Deployment Choices]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size:0.85em;"}
- Transformer blocks blend multi-head attention, feed-forward layers, residuals, and norms to build deep token representations  
- Fine-tuning general LLMs on medical corpora yields specialized, more accurate clinical models  
- Vigilance required for hallucinations, bias, and strict data privacy in healthcare  
- Chat interfaces for interactive Q&A; APIs for automation, integration, and scaling  
:::

::: notes
In Part 3, we unraveled how Transformer blocks work internally and how multi-head attention and feed-forward networks create rich token embeddings. We then examined the importance of adapting general LLMs to the medical domain while confronting potential pitfalls like hallucinations, bias, and privacy breaches. Finally, we compared chat-based and API-based deployments, providing guidance on selecting the best interface for your clinical or laboratory workflows.
:::
:::
